newsitem.title: USA: Tandem president charged in soft money scheme.
newsitem.headline: Tandem president charged in soft money scheme.

text.p: The president of Tandem Management Inc., a Manhattan-based investment advisory firm, has been indicted for his role in a scheme to misuse "soft dollar" commissions paid by the firm's clients to securities brokers, federal prosecutors said Thursday.

The indictment is part of a widening probe by federal authorities into alleged abuses of "soft dollar" practices. In a soft dollar arrangement, a money manager may cause clients to pay higher commission fees for trades executed by a brokerage firm to cover investment related services such as research reports.
Although the practice is not illegal, authorities are concerned that the fees are not always used to pay for costs associated with investment decisions.

In the case announced Thursday, William Branston, 41, of Long Island, New York, was charged with one count of conspiracy, nine counts of investment advisory fraud, two counts of wire fraud, three counts of filing false statements with the Securities and Exchange Commission and one count of perjury.
Each count carries a possible maximum sentence of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.
Branston's lawyer could not immediately be reached for comment.
Manhattan U.S. Attorney Mary Jo White also announced that Branston's former partners Eugene Deveney and Peter Alsop pleaded guilty last month for conspiring with Branston to defraud clients.
The charges against Branston allege that he and his partners ran schemes between 1991 and 1995 to defraud clients and obtain money for themselves.
In one scheme they allegedly gave clients and potential clients marketing materials that misrepresented Tandem's historical performance in managing client assets.
In another scheme they allegedly misused thousands of dollars of clients funds that they said were being used to obtain "soft dollar" services from brokerage firms.

Brokers who provide "soft dollar" services typically set aside a percentage of the commissions charged for trades as a credit or rebate that may be used by the customers to purchase "soft dollar" services.

In Tandem's case, brokers agreed to permit the firm to use the soft dollar credits by buying goods and services from vendors of its choice and then submitting the invoices for those items to the broker for reimbursement.

The indictment alleged that Branston and other employees caused brokers to reimburse Tandem or themselves in cash for hundreds of thousands of dollars of "soft dollar" expenses that had either already been reimbursed or never incurred.
The indictment alleged Branston was able to do this by submitting the same invoice, altered invoices or fictitious invoices to more than one broker so he could obtain multiple reimbursements.

It is also alleged that when a brokerage firm agreed to rebate in cash over half of the commissions paid by Tandem's clients for brokerage services, Branston and others kept the money instead of returning it to clients.
